categories.name: Human Spaceflight
categories.description: How people live, work, and stay safe beyond Earth.

articles.title: Crew Roles in a Space Station Mission
articles.summary: A station mission depends on coordinated roles, clear communication, and shared responsibility for safety.

sections.heading: Specialists, not solo heroes
body: Space station crews work as teams. Members may specialize in command, flight engineering, science, medicine, or other areas, but everyone contributes to housekeeping, maintenance, and safety.

A Crew Operations Support Officer supports the human side of the mission: schedules, crew readiness, resources, and communication. The role in this platform is an educational simulation role, not an official NASA position.

sections.heading: Training builds shared mental models
body: Crews train for normal operations, emergencies, and the unexpected. Repetition and realistic simulations help team members share an understanding of roles, procedures, and risks.
The Academy and mission simulator on this platform use that same learning pattern: study the science, then apply it to decisions with consequences.

articles.source_note: General NASA human spaceflight and station education concepts.

categories.name: Astronaut Health
categories.description: Whole-body health monitoring before, during, and after spaceflight.

articles.title: Monitoring Crew Health Without Inventing Numbers
articles.summary: Health monitoring combines crew reports, clinical checks, exercise records, sleep information, and environmental data.

sections.heading: Trends matter
body: A single measurement rarely tells the whole story. Crew health monitoring looks at trends over time: how sleep is changing, how exercise is tolerated, how nutrition and hydration are going, and whether mood or communication has shifted.
In this platform, systems use qualitative statuses rather than invented measurements. That reflects an educational boundary: a simulation should not pretend to know a crew member's clinical values.

sections.heading: Escalation is part of care
body: Crew members and support teams need clear pathways for raising a concern. Early support can prevent a small problem from becoming a mission-limiting one.
Nothing on this platform is a diagnosis or treatment. Real health questions belong with qualified medical professionals.

articles.source_note: Summarized from NASA Human Research Program themes.

categories.name: Sleep and Circadian Rhythm
categories.description: How light, schedule, and fatigue shape crew performance.

articles.title: Why Sleep Is a Mission System
articles.summary: Sleep supports attention, memory, mood, immunity, and metabolism. In orbit, the normal light-dark cycle is disrupted.

sections.heading: A day without a normal day
body: The space station orbits Earth roughly every 90 minutes, producing many sunrises and sunsets in 24 hours. The crew's internal clock still expects a daily rhythm, so schedules and lighting must compensate.
A protected sleep opportunity is not a luxury. It is a countermeasure that supports safe performance.

sections.heading: Fatigue is cumulative
body: Several short nights can create sleep debt. A tired crew member may not notice reduced vigilance, and self-report alone can miss risk. Team check-ins, sleep logs, and schedule review add useful information.
Caffeine and naps can support short-term alertness, but they do not replace core sleep.

articles.source_note: NASA-informed sleep and circadian education concepts.

categories.name: Exercise in Space
categories.description: Protecting bone, muscle, heart, and mission capability through loading.

articles.title: Exercise as a Countermeasure
articles.summary: Station crews use resistance and aerobic exercise to replace some of the loading that gravity normally provides.

sections.heading: Unloading changes the body
body: Without the continuous load of standing and moving against gravity, bone and muscle can lose capacity. The cardiovascular system also adapts to the changed environment.
Exercise hardware is engineered for weightlessness. A resistance device provides loading, a treadmill uses a harness to keep the crew member in place, and a cycle ergometer supports aerobic work.

sections.heading: Equipment is part of the plan
body: A faulty device is a safety and readiness issue. The response is to stop use, document the fault, use approved alternatives, and arrange inspection.
NASA schedules substantial exercise time for crews, commonly around two hours per day including setup. Individual plans vary and are monitored by the crew's health team.

categories.name: Space Nutrition
categories.description: Food systems, nutrients, hydration, and the morale of eating well.

articles.title: Food That Supports the Mission
articles.summary: Space food must be safe, shelf-stable, contained, and acceptable to the crew.

sections.heading: Engineering meets nutrition
body: Food is packaged to prevent crumbs and spills in weightlessness. Shelf-stable and rehydratable foods make up much of the menu, with fresh foods available occasionally.
Nutrition planning balances energy, protein, carbohydrate, fat, vitamins, minerals, and water with what the crew will actually eat. Variety and familiar foods support intake and morale.

sections.heading: Do not cut nutrition by default
body: When exercise is reduced temporarily, cutting portions is not a general solution. Crew members still need adequate energy and hydration, with attention to supportive nutrients such as protein, calcium, and vitamin D.
Food safety matters in a closed environment. Compromised packaging and unusual food conditions should be reported.

articles.source_note: NASA space food and crew nutrition education concepts.

categories.name: Mental Health
categories.description: Communication, resilience, workload, and support in isolated teams.

articles.title: Supporting the Human Side of Spaceflight
articles.summary: Isolation, confinement, workload, and uncertainty create predictable psychological demands.

sections.heading: Normal stress in an unusual place
body: A crew lives in a small environment with limited privacy and a fixed set of people. Ordinary frustrations can be amplified, and separation from family can be difficult.
These are environmental and human factors, not evidence that a crew member is weak. Clear information, meaningful work, connection with home, and predictable routines support resilience.

sections.heading: Talk early, support appropriately
body: Shared mental models, psychological safety, and structured conflict resolution help teams function. A facilitated conversation can repair communication before it becomes a safety issue.
Self-help strategies are useful, but persistent distress requires professional support. This platform provides education, not diagnosis or treatment.

articles.source_note: NASA behavioral health and team performance education themes.

categories.name: Hygiene in Space
categories.description: Low-water personal care, cleaning, and microbial control.

articles.title: Clean Without a Shower
articles.summary: Crews use rinse-free products, wipes, airflow, and careful waste handling instead of traditional showers.

sections.heading: Water behaves differently
body: In microgravity, water does not fall or pool the way it does on Earth. Hygiene uses controlled amounts of water, rinse-free products, and wipes, with airflow to manage moisture.
Water is recovered and reused within a shared system. Sequencing hygiene demand and reporting anomalies protects the whole crew.

sections.heading: A closed environment connects everyone
body: Shared surfaces, airflow, and waste handling influence the microbial environment. Cleaning schedules and hand hygiene reduce the chance that a small contamination becomes a shared problem.
Personal care is also about dignity and morale. Privacy, predictable routines, and crew preferences matter.

articles.source_note: NASA station hygiene and life-support education concepts.

categories.name: Microgravity
categories.description: How the body and materials behave when gravity's pull is removed.

articles.title: A Whole-Body Adaptation
articles.summary: Fluids shift, balance cues conflict, and bone and muscle lose loading in microgravity.

sections.heading: Fluids move upward
body: Without gravity pulling fluids toward the feet, body fluids shift toward the head. Crew members may notice facial puffiness or nasal congestion. The body adjusts over time.
Researchers study how fluid shift and pressure changes relate to eye and vision findings in some astronauts. Vision changes require professional monitoring.

sections.heading: Movement and return
body: The vestibular system receives conflicting signals during early adaptation, which can contribute to nausea or disorientation. Handrails, slow movement, and visual references help.
After return to gravity, the body must readapt again. Balance, blood pressure, and strength may need structured reconditioning.

categories.name: Space Station Systems
categories.description: The life-support, power, and equipment systems behind daily operations.

articles.title: A System of Systems
articles.summary: A station keeps people alive through interconnected atmosphere, water, power, thermal, and equipment systems.

sections.heading: Life support is integrated
body: Atmosphere monitoring, oxygen generation, carbon-dioxide removal, water recovery, and thermal control work together. A change in one area can affect another.
The mission simulator uses qualitative statuses for these systems. It does not invent oxygen, water, or power quantities.

sections.heading: Maintenance is continuous
body: Filters, pumps, exercise devices, and other equipment need inspection and repair. Crews follow procedures, document faults, and coordinate maintenance with the operations schedule.
A status dashboard is a summary, not a substitute for a proper inspection.

articles.source_note: NASA station systems education concepts, simplified for a qualitative simulation.

categories.name: Radiation Awareness
categories.description: Why radiation is a spaceflight consideration and how protection is planned.

articles.title: Time, Distance, and Shielding
articles.summary: Radiation protection uses the same broad principles in space as on Earth, applied to a different environment.

sections.heading: The space environment
body: Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field provide substantial protection at the surface. Crews in low Earth orbit are still exposed to a different radiation environment than people on the ground, and missions farther from Earth face different conditions.
Solar particle events can change the radiation environment quickly. Monitoring and protection planning are part of mission operations.

sections.heading: Protection is layered
body: Shielding, limiting time in higher-exposure areas, and increasing distance from a source are protective concepts. A spacecraft's structure and stowage can provide shielding in some areas.
This platform uses qualitative radiation statuses. It does not provide dose estimates or real operational thresholds, and it must not be used for actual mission planning.

articles.source_note: General NASA radiation education concepts; no operational values provided.

categories.name: Mars Exploration
categories.description: NASA missions, landing regions, and the tools used to explore Mars.

articles.title: Landing Regions and Rover Science
articles.summary: Jezero Crater and Gale Crater are real Mars landing regions with distinct scientific stories.

sections.heading: Jezero Crater
body: NASA's Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater on February 18, 2021. The region contains evidence of an ancient river delta and lake system. The mission seeks signs of ancient microbial life and is collecting samples for possible future return.
Jezero is not just a landing spot; it is a place to read the history of water and habitability on early Mars.

sections.heading: Gale Crater
body: NASA's Curiosity rover landed in Gale Crater in 2012. It has explored sedimentary layers around Mount Sharp, revealing a record of ancient environments that could have supported microbial life.
Mars Trek lets you explore these regions using NASA map data and imagery. The platform does not invent coordinates or scientific observations; use the official layers and mission pages.

articles.source_note: NASA Mars mission facts. Open official sources for current details.

categories.name: Planetary Science
categories.description: Reading planets through geology, atmospheres, and comparative worlds.

articles.title: How Scientists Read a Planet
articles.summary: Planetary science combines images, spectra, topography, chemistry, and comparative planetology.

sections.heading: Multiple lines of evidence
body: A single image can suggest a story, but scientists test it with other data: mineral signatures, elevation, sediment layers, chemistry, and the context of the surrounding landscape.
Mars Trek provides access to NASA map layers and imagery. Use the official tools to observe, compare, and ask questions rather than assuming a feature's origin from one view.

sections.heading: Earth is a reference, not a copy
body: Comparing Mars with Earth helps scientists understand processes such as volcanism, erosion, and sedimentation. But Mars has its own history, atmosphere, and conditions.
Planetary science is an exercise in evidence and uncertainty. Good observations are paired with clear questions and honest limits.

articles.source_note: General NASA planetary science education concepts.
